$comment: Single source of truth for every file the browser loads to run a model: the model weights and tokenizers, the ONNX Runtime wasm and its JS glue. Each file is pinned by size and SHA-256. scripts/fetch-models.mjs checks them at build time; the app checks them again in the browser (src/ml/verify.ts) before use and refuses a file that does not match. Everything is served from our own origin under /models/. Nothing here may point at another host. Adding a model means adding it here first; a file that is not listed is never loaded.

runtime.$comment: cpu-wasm and webgpu-wasm are fetched from /models/ort/ and checked in the browser. The CPU JS glue is code that ONNX Runtime import()s (and starts its pthread workers from) by URL, and the page's CSP has no blob:, so the browser cannot hand it bytes it checked. It is therefore NOT served from /models/: it is built INTO the app (worker.ts imports it with ?url, Vite emits it as a content-hashed file under /assets/ next to the JavaScript), and its pin below is checked at build time (vite.config.ts, scripts/fetch-models.mjs) and in the build audit (scripts/audit-web-build.mjs). Its trust is the app's own JavaScript (W4), not a browser-side check.

models.$comment: The English text-recognition data for tesseract.js (Apache-2.0 tessdata_best, integer-quantised LSTM). Not downloaded: scripts/fetch-models.mjs copies it from the installed npm package (source), which must match this pin. The OCR CODE (the tesseract.js worker script and its WebAssembly core) cannot be checked in the browser, because the browser starts a worker from a URL and the core is run by importScripts, so both are built INTO the app instead (bundled: content-hashed files under /assets/, checked at build time by vite.config.ts, scripts/fetch-models.mjs and scripts/audit-web-build.mjs). Only the language data goes through the browser-side check (src/ml/verify.ts) and is handed to the worker as bytes. The file is gzip data, served under a .bin name on purpose: a static server that sees .gz may add Content-Encoding: gzip, the browser would then decompress it before the hash check, and the pinned bytes would never match. The engine recognises gzip by its first bytes, not its name.
